title: Framing decriminalization: A mixed-methods study on media narratives, government resources, misinformation, and public support of British Columbia's drug decriminalization policy
screen_reason: Mixed-methods study whose content-analysis arm codes 98 government resources and 301 media articles for misinformation and for misleading content against official and peer-reviewed sources, reporting four item-level shares with denominators: 9% of government resources and 34% of media articles contained misinformation; 1% of government resources and 21% of media articles contained misleading content. These are shares of items judged for truth/falsity against an external ground truth, so CONTENT. The survey arm (1,200 BC residents) measured information SOURCES, support and perceived safety, not self-reported misinformation exposure, so it yields no RECALL row.

estimates.country: Canada (British Columbia policy); media corpus includes Canadian national (37%), BC provincial (32%), international (16%) and other-provincial (15%) outlets
estimates.platform: News media websites (Canadian and international), retrieved through general and advanced Google search filtered to the News tab
estimates.date: Articles published online 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025; corpus collected 29 April - 24 June 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of news media articles about BC's drug decriminalization policy that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 301 media articles discussing BC's decriminalization policy or its amendment, published online 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025 (770 records screened, 318 met inclusion criteria, 17 dropped during coding for lack of analysable content; syndicated duplicates counted once)
estimates.definition: Article containing at least one factually incorrect claim about the policy's design, scope or outcomes that could be objectively verified as false - e.g. incorrect statements about policy intent/goals, an incorrect possession threshold, conflating decriminalization with legalization, misstatements about enforcement rules, incorrect dates, unsubstantiated negative outcomes, or misrepresentation of implementation status
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation refers to false or inaccurate information that is shared without the deliberate intention of misleading readers, whereas misleading content is factually accurate information that is presented in a manner that creates confusion or distorts the surrounding context."
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was identified in 34 % (n = 103/301) of media articles, and when broken down by article stance, was disproportionately concentrated in oppositional coverage. Specifically, 58 % (n = 48/83) of oppositional articles, 34 % (n = 46/134) of neutral articles, and 11 % (n = 9/84) of supportive articles contained misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results > Content accuracy: identifying misinformation and misleading narratives > Media articles, p. 9; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Inductively developed codebook refined on a jointly coded calibration subset of 35 articles (FA, SCP, JMG); two trained coders (JMG, SCP) then divided the full set and coded independently; the lead author (FA) reviewed every article flagged as containing misinformation or misleading content to confirm coding accuracy; discrepancies resolved by team consensus. Claims were 'systematically cross-checked against credible sources, including the Government of BC and Health Canada reports ... as well as relevant peer-reviewed publications'. NO inter-coder reliability statistic (no kappa or percent agreement) is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: In this study, misinformation included factually incorrect claims about the policy's design, scope, or outcomes that could be objectively verified as false (e.g., asserting that decriminalization legalized all drugs) ... To ensure accuracy, all claims from media and government sources were systematically cross-checked against credible sources, including the Government of BC and Health Canada reports (Government of BC, 2025b; Health Canada, 2024), as well as relevant peer-reviewed publications available.
estimates.notes: year set to 2023, the midpoint of the 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025 publication window and the modal period (52% of articles fell between implementation in January 2023 and the May 2024 amendment); the corpus itself was retrieved in April-June 2025. Stance sub-shares are recorded in value_raw rather than as separate rows because stance is a within-corpus content category, not the paper's headline population split. Note the internal inconsistency in the paper's own stance arithmetic: 48 + 46 + 9 = 103 matches, but the sentence 'Among all articles containing misinformation (n = 103), nearly half (n = 46/103; 45 %) were neutral in stance, followed by 23 % (n = 24/103) oppositional' contradicts the 48 oppositional articles reported one sentence earlier (24 is the count that misrepresented policy intent). I used the 48/83 figure. quote_verbatim=false: the sentence is transcribed faithfully but the PDF text breaks it with line-break hyphenation ('media ar-ticles') and a spacing artefact ('(n =3/ 9'), so it is not byte-identical to the extracted text file.

estimates.country: Canada (British Columbia policy); media corpus includes Canadian national (37%), BC provincial (32%), international (16%) and other-provincial (15%) outlets
estimates.platform: News media websites (Canadian and international), retrieved through general and advanced Google search filtered to the News tab
estimates.date: Articles published online 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025; corpus collected 29 April - 24 June 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of news media articles about BC's drug decriminalization policy that contained misleading content (factually accurate but contextually distorted)
estimates.value_raw: 63/301 (21%) [exact 20.9%]; by stance: oppositional 44/63 (70%), neutral 14/63 (22%), supportive 5/63 (8%) of the misleading articles
estimates.denominator: 301 media articles discussing BC's decriminalization policy or its amendment, published online 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025
estimates.definition: Article containing factually manipulative or contextually distorted content that misleads readers by omitting key context or oversimplifying/subtly exaggerating connections - implied causality (linking the policy to increased crime, overdose rates, public drug use, health harms or death), headline/image sensationalism, or other misleading framing
estimates.misinfo_def: "misleading content is factually accurate information that is presented in a manner that creates confusion or distorts the surrounding context" ... "technically accurate statements that distorted meaning through selective reporting, implied inflated outcomes, or the omission of key context (e.g., attributing rising overdose deaths and hospitalizations to decriminalization without supporting evidence)"
estimates.source_quote: Misleading content was identified in 21 % (n = 63/301) of all media articles. When disaggregated by article stance, oppositional articles accounted for the highest proportion of misleading content (n = 44/63; 70 %), followed by neutral (n = 14/63; 22 %) and supportive articles (n = 5/63; 8 %).
estimates.page_loc: Results > Content accuracy > Media articles, p. 9
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same procedure and coders as the misinformation row: inductive codebook, 35-article calibration set jointly coded by FA/SCP/JMG, independent coding by JMG and SCP, lead-author review of every flagged article, consensus resolution, cross-checking against Government of BC and Health Canada reports and peer-reviewed publications. No kappa reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Types of Misleading Content*: Factually manipulative or contextually distorted content that misleads readers by omitting key context, and/or oversimplifying or subtly exaggerating connections. Includes: - Implied causality (e.g. misleading narratives linking policy to increased crime, overdose rates, public drug use, or resulting in health harms/risks or death) - Headline/image sensationalism ... - Other misleading framing
estimates.notes: definition_variant = true: this is the same 301-article corpus under the paper's BROADER, separately coded label ('misleading content', explicitly defined as factually ACCURATE information distorted by framing or omission), so it must not be pooled with the 34% misinformation row - the two categories are separately coded and can overlap in the same article; the paper never reports a combined 'misinformation OR misleading' share, and computing one would violate R8 (cross-category sum).

estimates.country: Canada (British Columbia); federal Government of Canada, Government of BC and BC regional health authority sources
estimates.platform: Government and regional health authority websites (webpages, reports, news/press releases, knowledge-translation tools such as infographics and posters)
estimates.date: Resources published online 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025; corpus collected 29 April - 24 June 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of public-facing government resources about BC's drug decriminalization policy that contained misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 9/98 (9%) [exact 9.2%]; distributed equally across educational (3/9), outcome-focused (3/9) and broader-publication (3/9) resources; by source: health authority 6/9 (67%), provincial government 3/9 (33%), federal 0/15 resources
estimates.denominator: 98 public-facing government resources discussing BC's decriminalization policy, published online 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025 (969 records screened, 100 met inclusion criteria, 2 dropped during coding); 51 from provincial health authority websites, 32 from the BC provincial government site, 15 from the federal government site
estimates.definition: Resource containing at least one factually incorrect claim about the policy's design, scope or outcomes objectively verifiable as false; the most frequent form was misrepresenting the policy's intent and goals (5/9), notably the false assertion that public drug use was permitted, followed by conflating decriminalization with legalization (3/9) and claiming police could not intervene in public substance use (2/9)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation refers to false or inaccurate information that is shared without the deliberate intention of misleading readers, whereas misleading content is factually accurate information that is presented in a manner that creates confusion or distorts the surrounding context."
estimates.source_quote: Among the 98 government resources, 9 % (n = 9/98) contained misinformation, distributed equally across educational resources (n = 3/9; 33 %), outcome-focused resources (n = 3/9; 33 %), and in broader publications where decriminalization was discussed as a secondary focus (n = 3/9; 33 %).
estimates.page_loc: Results > Content accuracy > Government resources, p. 9; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same coding team and procedure as the media rows; claims cross-checked against Government of BC and Health Canada reports and peer-reviewed publications; lead author reviewed every flagged resource; consensus resolution; no kappa reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Guided by this conceptual framework, we performed a systematic search of the websites of the Government of Canada, the Government of BC, and BC's regional health authorities, using predetermined search terms (e.g. 'drug decriminalization').
estimates.notes: This is a distinct cell from the media rows: a different source class (official government/health-authority material rather than news media) on the same topic and in the same country, so it is a separate estimate rather than a definition variant. The corpus is a comprehensive keyword search of a defined set of official websites, so denom_selection is left blank rather than curated. quote_verbatim=false: the sentence is transcribed faithfully but the PDF text breaks it with line-break hyphenation ('media ar-ticles') and a spacing artefact ('(n =3/ 9'), so it is not byte-identical to the extracted text file.

estimates.source_quote: Minimal misleading content was identified in government resources, with only one instance (n = 1/98; 1 %) observed. This case, found in an educational resource, stated that decriminalization made communities unsafe and framed this as justification for recriminalizing possession in most public spaces.
estimates.page_loc: Results > Content accuracy > Government resources, p. 9
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same coding team and procedure as the other rows; no kappa reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Types of Misleading Content*: Factually manipulative or contextually distorted content that misleads readers by omitting key context, and/or oversimplifying or subtly exaggerating connections.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted. (a) The 1,200-respondent Ipsos survey of BC adults measured which information SOURCES respondents used (TV/radio 51%, news websites 38%, direct conversations 31%, social media 27%, government sites 18%, none 9%), policy support (47% did not support, 28% support, 19% neutral) and perceived safety (47% felt less safe). None of these is a self-reported share of respondents who encountered misinformation, so there is no RECALL row - the review's RECALL construct requires a share reporting exposure to misinformation, not to information in general. (b) Stance shares of the 301 articles (neutral 45%, supportive 28%, oppositional 28%) and the reason/messenger breakdowns (e.g. politicians cited in 80% of articles) are framing and sourcing categories, not veracity. (c) Within-misinformation composition (types of misinformation: policy intent 63/103 = 61%, unsubstantiated outcomes 30/103 = 29%; misleading types: crime narratives 25/63 = 40%, health risks 25/63 = 40%) is composition inside the misinformation set, not prevalence, so no within_misinfo_content rows were created. (d) Temporal shares (e.g. 13% of dated government resources released before implementation) are timing, not veracity. (e) The stance-specific misinformation shares (58% oppositional, 34% neutral, 11% supportive) are recorded in value_raw of the media row but not as separate rows, since article stance is a content category rather than the paper's headline population split. (f) One internal inconsistency worth an adjudicator's eye: the paper reports 48/83 oppositional articles with misinformation, then says only 23% (24/103) of misinformation-containing articles were oppositional; 24 is elsewhere the count of oppositional articles misrepresenting policy intent, so the second sentence appears to be an error. It does not affect the 34% headline.

rob.design: Two-stage exploratory mixed-methods design. CONTENT ARM: systematic searches of Government of Canada, Government of BC and BC regional health authority websites with predetermined and iteratively expanded search terms, plus general and advanced Google searches filtered to the News tab for media articles; inclusion window 31 May 2022 - 31 May 2025; data collected 29 April - 24 June 2025; user-generated content and passing mentions excluded; syndicated duplicates catalogued but counted once. PRISMA-style flow: 969 government records to 100 included to 98 analysed; 770 media records to 318 included to 301 analysed. Inductive codebook developed through team discussion; 35-article calibration set jointly coded by three team members (FA, SCP, JMG); then two trained coders (JMG, SCP) split the corpus and coded independently; lead author (FA) reviewed all items flagged for misinformation or misleading content; discrepancies resolved by consensus. NO inter-coder reliability statistic reported. Claims cross-checked against Government of BC and Health Canada reports and peer-reviewed publications. SURVEY ARM: cross-sectional online survey administered by Ipsos in February 2025 to English-speaking BC adults 18+, non-probability quota sampling by gender, age, region and education with rim post-stratification weighting to census proportions; 6,680 recruited, 507 ineligible, 1,269 excluded after quotas filled, 4,904 eligible, 169 incomplete, final n = 1,200, response rate 25% among eligible. Rao-Scott chi-square and logistic regression adjusted for age and gender, weighted procedures in SAS 9.4; the authors state these findings are meant to complement rather than explain the content analysis given the non-probability design. Ethics: CAMH REB 2023/173 for the survey; the content analysis required no review (public secondary sources).
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation refers to false or inaccurate information that is shared without the deliberate intention of misleading readers, whereas misleading content is factually accurate information that is presented in a manner that creates confusion or distorts the surrounding context (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2024; Ruokolainen et al., 2023). In this study, misinformation included factually incorrect claims about the policy's design, scope, or outcomes that could be objectively verified as false (e.g., asserting that decriminalization legalized all drugs), while misleading content referred to technically accurate statements that distorted meaning through selective reporting, implied inflated outcomes, or the omission of key context.
rob.item10_quote: Misinformation was identified in 34 % (n = 103/301) of media articles ... Among the 98 government resources, 9 % (n = 9/98) contained misinformation.
